newsitem.title: UK: Copper spins lower on LME, market ends weak.
newsitem.headline: Copper spins lower on LME, market ends weak.

text.p: Copper prices came under severe pressure in active Thursday afternoon LME trading, as earlier declines under $2,000 were extended significantly.
Important chart support levels were brushed aside by the weight of liquidation, fund sales and option selling, putting thr market on course to test $1,920 in the first instance and then $1,900.
"This is a market under pressure. The spreads are easing, there is little real offtake, and the option boys are driving things," one trader said.
Recent wide price movements, with the market rising to 2-1/2 month highs around $2,165 a tonne this week then rapidly retreating, highlight the influence of both LME and off-market Asian options.

Delta hedge cover is put in place then unwound, increasing option volatility and exaggerating underlying price movements. Also, investment funds have looked to play the market, riding the trend and extending the price moves, they added.

Meanwhile, fears of September date tightness have proved to be illusory, with backwardations subsiding this week. Cash to the third Wednesday September date is now around $2 backwardation, while cash to three months has contracted to a $5/10 premium.
On Wednesday, cash/threes was at a $20 premium and has been as high as $60 this week. Traders say many September short positions have been squared off or rolled forward.
Three months prices, at a peak of $2,037 a tonne this morning, finished the kerb at $1,925, down $95 a tonne from Wednesday.
Other LME metals were largely carried along by copper's weakness, and broke lower this afternoon.
"At the moment it is all about copper. If that falls then there is not much to hold the others," another trader said.

Aluminium crumbled under $1,500, but there was little heavy selling and last business was at $1,492, down $16. There is likely to be support around $1,470, while late news of Alcoa's labour problems will also induce caution.

Nickel prices clawed their way hesitantly back to the $7,500 level, but the market outlook remained weak, given copper's losses. Three months bottomed out at $7,420 before ending the kerb at $7,500, down $50.
Lead was partially supported by November tightness, but eventually tracked lower with copper and closed at a softer $813/14 a tonne.
Zinc managed to hold in its new technical range of $1,040/50, but is likely to come under renewed downside pressure in the short-term. Last business was at $1,040, up $2.
Tin subsided in line with the main trend and closed at $6,225 a tonne, down $30. Alloy was marked lower, closing at $1,280/90.
